title: Diabetes in pregnancy: pregestational vs GDM, White classification, glycemic targets, insulin and fetal surveillance
subject: ss-obg
refs: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 190: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care in Diabetes (2024)

steps.say: Pregnancy induces profound physiological insulin resistance driven by placental endocrine secretion. Human placental lactogen, human placental growth hormone, progesterone, and cortisol elevate circulating maternal free fatty acids to spare glucose for transplacental facilitated diffusion.
steps.tx: Pregnancy-induced physiological insulin resistance is mediated by placental hormones including **human placental lactogen** (hPL), growth hormone, progesterone, and cortisol. These hormones induce maternal peripheral **insulin resistance** and promote lipolysis, preserving a concentration gradient for maternal-fetal **glucose transfer** via placental GLUT-1 transporters.

steps.say: International guidelines establish rigorous diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus using a standardized 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test. Under IADPSG criteria, a fasting plasma glucose of 92, a one-hour level of 180, or a two-hour level of 153 milligrams per deciliter establishes the diagnosis.
steps.tx: The single-step **IADPSG criteria** using a 75 g **oral glucose tolerance test** establishes **gestational diabetes** if any single value meets or exceeds the following thresholds: **fasting blood glucose** >= 92 mg/dL, 1-hour plasma glucose >= 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour plasma glucose >= 153 mg/dL.

steps.say: Pre-gestational diabetes requires clinical stratification to quantify maternal microvascular risk and perinatal prognosis. Priscilla White's classification categorizes gestational diabetes into diet-controlled Class A1 and insulin-requiring Class A2, while designating vascular nephropathy as Class F and proliferative retinopathy as Class R.
steps.tx: The **White classification** stratifies diabetes in pregnancy: Class A1 represents diet-controlled GDM, Class A2 requires pharmacotherapy, Class B has onset >= 20 years with duration < 10 years, Class C has onset 10 to 19 years, Class D has duration > 20 years, **Class F** denotes diabetic nephropathy, and **Class R** denotes **proliferative retinopathy**.

nodes.label: Gestational onset diabetes: Class A1 (diet-managed) vs Class A2 (medication)
Pregestational without microvascular disease: Class B (>= 20y onset) and Class C (10-19y)
Pregestational with benign retinopathy: Class D (> 20y duration or background changes)
High-risk microvascular disease: Class F (nephropathy), Class R (retinopathy), Class H (cardiac)

steps.say: Strict glycemic regulation minimizes maternal morbidity and halts excessive fetal growth acceleration. Clinical targets require maintaining fasting glucose below 95 milligrams per deciliter, one-hour postprandial glucose under 140, and two-hour postprandial glucose under 120 milligrams per deciliter.
steps.tx: Tight maternal **glycemic targets** demand maintaining **fasting glucose** < 95 mg/dL, **1-hour postprandial** glucose < 140 mg/dL, and **2-hour postprandial** glucose < 120 mg/dL, with target glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) maintained strictly < 6.0 percent to prevent accelerated fetal growth, macrosomia, and polyhydramnios.

steps.say: Pedersen's classic hypothesis explains the origin of perinatal metabolic complications. Maternal hyperglycemia drives excess glucose across the placenta, stimulating fetal pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia. The resulting fetal hyperinsulinemia accelerates glycogen synthesis, organomegaly, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.
steps.tx: The **Pedersen hypothesis** explains diabetic fetopathy: maternal hyperglycemia triggers transplacental glucose overload, stimulating fetal pancreatic **beta-cell hyperplasia** and excessive **fetal hyperinsulinemia**, which drives excessive somatic fat accumulation, hepatic glycogen storage, **fetal macrosomia**, and profound neonatal hypoglycemia immediately following cord clamping.

left.title: Maternal Hyperglycemic State
points: Elevated maternal plasma glucose crosses placenta via GLUT-1
Maternal insulin does NOT cross the placenta
Elevated amino acids and ketones co-transported

right.title: Fetal Hyperinsulinemic Sequelae
points: Fetal pancreatic beta-cells produce massive insulin surge
Acts as potent growth hormone stimulating macrosomia and organomegaly
Sudden cut of glucose supply at birth causes profound neonatal hypoglycemia

steps.say: First-trimester periconceptional hyperglycemia acts as a potent teratogen during organogenesis. Caudal regression syndrome, also termed sacral agenesis, is 200 times more prevalent in pregestational diabetes, alongside transposition of the great arteries, ventricular septal defects, and neural tube anomalies.
steps.tx: Poor periconceptional glycemic control (HbA1c > 8 to 10 percent) causes severe congenital malformations: **caudal regression syndrome** (sacral agenesis) is the most specific anomaly, while **ventricular septal defect**, transposition of the great arteries, and **neural tube defects** are the most common.

left.title: Most Specific Diabetic Anomaly
points: Relative risk increased > 200-fold in pregestational diabetes
Features hypoplastic lower extremities and sacral agenesis

right.title: Most Common Malformations
points: Central nervous system defects (anencephaly, spina bifida)
Renal anomalies (hydronephrosis, renal agenesis, duplex systems)

steps.say: Insulin remains the first-line pharmacotherapeutic agent when medical nutritional therapy fails to achieve glycemic control. Clinicians calculate starting doses based on gestational weight and trimester, employing basal-bolus regimens with rapid-acting analogs like lispro or aspart and intermediate NPH or detemir.
steps.tx: When nutritional therapy fails, **insulin therapy** serves as the gold standard medication. Total daily requirement increases progressively across pregnancy (0.7 U/kg in first trimester, 0.8 U/kg in second, and 0.9 to 1.0 U/kg in third trimester), divided into a **basal-bolus regimen** using **insulin lispro** or aspart and **NPH insulin**.

nodes.label: Assess failed glycemic targets on medical nutrition therapy after 1 to 2 weeks
Calculate starting dose: 0.7 to 1.0 U/kg based on current gestational age
Distribute dose: 50% basal (NPH or detemir) and 50% prandial (lispro or aspart)
Divide prandial boluses into breakfast, lunch, and dinner based on blood glucose logs

steps.say: Delivery timing balances metabolic stillbirth risks against shoulder dystocia and neonatal respiratory distress. Well-controlled gestational diabetes delivers safely between 39 and 40 weeks, while medically treated pregnancies deliver between 37 and 39 weeks, offering elective cesarean if fetal weight exceeds 4500 grams.
steps.tx: Guidelines for **delivery timing** in diabetic pregnancy recommend delivery at 39 to 40 weeks for diet-controlled GDM, 37 to 39 weeks for insulin-managed diabetes, and offering elective **cesarean section** when estimated fetal weight exceeds **4500 grams** to eliminate catastrophic **shoulder dystocia**.
